title: Trump Told Axios He 'No Longer' Views Anthropic as a Threat — While Refusing to Rule Out Defense Production Act Emergency Powers over the Same Company. Commerce's 12 June Directive Cited Only 'Verbal Evidence' of a Single Jailbreak That Anthropic Has Technically Rebutted, Independent Analysts Called 'Baffling,' and the NSA Was Simultaneously Authorised to Use Mythos 5 for Offensive Cyber Operations Under Project Glasswing (22 June 2026)
narrative:
On 22 June 2026, U.S. President Donald Trump told the Axios Show he 'no longer' views Anthropic as a national security threat — 'well, not now, but a week ago, maybe.' The interview came ten days after the Commerce Department under Secretary Howard Lutnick issued an export-control letter to Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei directing that the company's two most advanced models — Fable 5 and Mythos 5 — be cut off from any foreign national, including foreign-national Anthropic employees inside the United States. Anthropic complied on the evening of 12 June by disabling both models for all customers.

Trump's framing presents the export-control directive as a resolved dispute. He characterised Amodei as having responded 'very quickly' and 'responsibly,' said he was 'grateful for the ongoing partnership,' and declined to rule out emergency powers under the Defense Production Act: 'I have the power to use a lot of things. But I'm not sure I have to do that.' The Anthropic spokesperson response described the dispute as an 'ongoing partnership' and a 'shared goal' of protecting critical infrastructure. The exchange took place at the G7 summit in France, where Trump and other G7 leaders met with tech bosses including Amodei. Anthropic's ongoing litigation against the Trump administration challenging its earlier Pentagon blacklisting remains active.

analysis:
The Anthropic story is a documentary-credibility piece in the same 'verbal evidence only' denial pattern documented in the prior Pantsir-missile / Moscow refinery (19 June), Krasnodar Poltavskaya (16 June), BBC Verify Iran (16 June), Bryansk bus (17 June), and NEET-UG NTA (22 June) stories — but for an export-control directive against a U.S. frontier-AI company with published technical rebuttal, paired with an internal-contradiction in the federal government's own posture toward the same model. Below the surface, five specific findings make the 22 June 2026 'no longer a threat' framing a beat-distinct piece from the surrounding verbal-evidence-only coverage.

**Finding 1 — The verbal-evidence basis is the load-bearing procedural finding.** The Commerce directive's only cited rationale is a 'narrow, non-universal jailbreak' that, per Anthropic, 'essentially consists of asking the model to read a specific codebase and fix any software flaws.' Anthropic's published rebuttal states the jailbreak is 'widely available from other models (including OpenAI's GPT-5.5), and is used every day by the defenders who keep systems safe.' The directive's only supporting evidence, per Anthropic and CyberScoop reporting, is verbal — 'To date, the government has only given us verbal evidence of a potential narrow, non-universal jailbreak.' No written technical report has been released. The 'another company' that allegedly 'claimed it was able to jailbreak Mythos' has not been named. The jailbreak demonstration has not been released. The chain of custody from the unnamed company to Commerce's decision has not been published. An export-control directive that disables two frontier models for all customers — exceeding the foreign-national scope of the directive itself — on the basis of verbal evidence of a single jailbreak that has not been published is the procedural finding.

**Finding 2 — The NSA / Project Glasswing internal contradiction is the structural finding.** Anthropic was placed on a Pentagon blacklist in February 2026 deeming it 'too dangerous for the government's own use.' In March 2026 — one month later — the NSA was given Mythos 5 to conduct offensive cyber operations under Project Glasswing. The same model was simultaneously too dangerous for federal agencies, safe enough for offensive NSA operations, and (per the 12 June directive) too dangerous for foreign-national access. The internal contradiction is structural: the federal government cannot coherently assert Mythos 5 is 'too dangerous for foreign-national Anthropic employees inside the United States' while authorising the same model for offensive cyber operations. The 'no longer a threat' framing does not address this internal contradiction.

**Finding 3 — The scope asymmetry is the procedural finding that exceeds the directive itself.** The Commerce directive applied to foreign nationals and foreign-national Anthropic employees inside the U.S. To ensure compliance, Anthropic disabled the models for all customers, including U.S. persons. The directive was restricted to foreigners; the compliance was universal. The asymmetric scope — directive restricted to foreigners, compliance universal — has not been publicly justified by either Commerce or Anthropic. The 'across-the-board disabling of all customer access,' per independent analyst Chris McGuire, is 'inconsistent with the underlying concern.' The standard procedural response — Commerce clarifying that U.S.-person access was not within scope, or Anthropic restoring U.S.-person access as a partial step — has not occurred. The asymmetric scope is itself the procedural consequence of a verbal-evidence basis: an agency that cannot publish the basis for the directive cannot tell a frontier-AI company how narrowly to comply with it.

**Finding 4 — The Defense Production Act non-denial is the unresolved-dispute signal.** Trump's 'I have the power to use a lot of things. But I'm not sure I have to do that' formulation is a non-denial of emergency powers over the same company whose dispute he described as resolved. If the export-control directive is the resolution, the Defense Production Act would not be in play. The DPA non-denial is the procedural signal that the dispute is paused, not resolved — paired with Anthropic's active litigation against the Trump administration challenging the prior Pentagon blacklisting. The 22 June exchange presents the dispute as a partnership while the litigation posture indicates it is not. The 'ongoing partnership' and 'shared goal' framing from Anthropic is the diplomatic register; the active litigation is the substantive register.

**Finding 5 — The independent-analyst consensus is the external-credibility finding.** Dean Ball, Foundation for American Innovation senior fellow, called the move 'baffling.' Chris McGuire noted the across-the-board disabling of all customer access 'inconsistent with the underlying concern.' No administration technical rebuttal has been released. The independent-analyst consensus — across both the AI-skeptical and AI-progressive wings of the Foundation for American Innovation orbit — is that the directive's rationale does not survive scrutiny. The 'no longer a threat' framing on 22 June does not engage with the analyst consensus; it presents the dispute as resolved at the political layer while the technical and procedural layers remain open. The pairing of 'partnership' framing with verbal-evidence-only basis is the structural finding: the political resolution does not address the documentary record.
verdict: The Anthropic story is a documentary-credibility piece built on the most aggressive export-control directive in the frontier-AI space — issued on the basis of verbal evidence of a single jailbreak that the affected company has technically rebutted, that independent analysts have called 'baffling,' and that has never been published. The same model was simultaneously authorised for NSA offensive-cyber use under Project Glasswing while being too dangerous for foreign-national access. Anthropic disabled the models for all customers to ensure compliance, exceeding the directive's foreign-national scope. The 'partnership' framing is paired with an explicit non-denial of the Defense Production Act — the dispute is procedurally paused, not substantively resolved. The active litigation against the Trump administration is the substantive register; the 22 June Axios exchange is the diplomatic register. Beat-distinct from prior verbal-evidence-only coverage (Pantsir, Krasnodar Poltavskaya, Moscow refinery, BBC Verify Iran, Bryansk bus, NTA NEET-UG) on the export-control / frontier-AI layer: this story does not have a denial layer that can be triangulated against independent OSINT; it has a published technical rebuttal from the affected company that the directive's verbal evidence has not addressed; an internal contradiction in the federal government's own posture toward the same model (Pentagon blacklist vs NSA Glasswing); and a scope asymmetry (foreign-national directive, universal compliance) that has not been publicly justified. The structural finding is the same model simultaneously too dangerous for foreigners, too dangerous for federal agencies, and safe enough for offensive U.S. cyber operations — paired with a 'no longer a threat' framing that does not engage with any of the documentary record on which the underlying directive was based.
